title: Why Straying From Your Classroom Management Plan Is A Gamble You'll Lose Every Time -plan-is-a-gamble/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin catalogs seven specific consequences of straying from a classroom management plan, even in seemingly minor or well-intentioned ways, such as overlooking a good student's slip-up or skipping a consequence because enforcing it feels inconvenient. The consequences include losing student trust, creating resentment over perceived favoritism, inviting escalating testing of boundaries, harming the class's best-behaved students, being driven back toward yelling and lecturing, and opening the door to broader misbehavior and distraction. He frames consistent enforcement as a kind of insurance policy that protects both the teacher's authority and the classroom's overall climate. The piece closes with an encouraging note that recommitting to the plan, even after a period of inconsistency, reliably produces improvement over time.
points: Even small, well-intentioned deviations from a classroom management plan compound into larger management problems.
Inconsistent enforcement breeds perceptions of favoritism and erodes student trust.
Giving in or losing emotional control invites students to test boundaries more frequently.
A class's best-behaved students are often the most harmed by inconsistent enforcement of the plan.
Recommitting to consistent enforcement, even after backsliding, produces steady improvement over time.
quotes: Following your classroom management plan isn’t always easy. But ignoring it is a gamble you’ll lose every time.
Once your students realize that you don’t always follow your classroom management plan, they’ll begin losing respect for you and trust in what you say.
When you’re inconsistent, your students will think you’re playing favorites. “Why did I get a warning for calling out, but she didn’t?” is a common refrain.
If you show a tendency to give in, to let things go, or to lose emotional control, then you’re going to be tested—more every day.
Teachers who forgo their plan find themselves needing to yell, scold, lecture, and the like in order to maintain control.
When you let even small things go, like the occasional calling out, it opens the floodgates to more misbehavior.
Decide to stop rolling the dice and start staying true to your word.
